ch01.note: The steel bridge across the mouth of Suzhou Creek where it joins the Huangpu, at the north end of the Bund; in the foreign settlements of the day it was known in English as the Garden Bridge. The whole drive that follows — over the bridge, down the Bund, west along Nanjing Road and out along what the settlement called Bubbling Well Road (the Jing'an Temple Road further on) to the western villa district — traces the real map of the International Settlement in 1930.

The Taishang Ganying Pian (太上感应篇), the “Tract of the Most High on Action and Response,” a short Daoist morality book usually dated to the Song dynasty, which teaches that every good or evil act draws an exact recompense from Heaven. For centuries it was among the most frequently reprinted of all Chinese religious texts, and was commonly printed and given away free as an act of merit, exactly as old Mr. Wu does here. Its best-known couplet is quoted a little further on.

Wenchang Dijun, the Daoist god of literature and of success in the imperial examinations, worshipped above all by the scholar class. The couplet that follows — “of all vices lust is the first, of all virtues filial piety comes first” — is a popular morality maxim of the sort such tracts spread, cited here as the Lord Wenchang's own teaching.

The “reform party” renders weixin dang, the reform current of the late Qing that culminated in the abortive Hundred Days' Reform of 1898; a “reform-party” man was a modernizing reformer. That old Mr. Wu's forebears were shilang (vice-ministers) of the imperial government, while he had once been a reformer and is now a Daoist recluse, sets up the novel's recurring motif of the conflict of the generations.

ch01.anchor: monster the Master would not speak of
ch01.note: An allusion to the Analects (Book VII): “The Master did not speak of prodigies, feats of strength, disorders, or spirits” (zi bu yu). To the old man the motor-car is exactly such an unspeakable prodigy.

Jintong yunü, the boy and girl who attend a Daoist immortal in popular iconography, emblems of unspoiled innocence. Old Mr. Wu casts his young daughter and son in these roles, which makes their swift corruption by Shanghai the sharper.

The crossing of Nanjing Road and Henan Road, long known by this name (literally “the ball-throwing ground,” after a recreation ground once on the spot); one of the busiest intersections of the International Settlement.
Fan Bowen reaches for a bookish classical phrase, shenshen er li, “to revile at length”; the stilted diction is of a piece with the affected poet he is drawn as.
A year in the sexagenary cycle by which years were traditionally reckoned; jiazi is the first of the sixty. The dating places the postscript in 1924.

ch02.note: The Whampoa Military Academy (黄埃军校), founded near Guangzhou in 1924 and headed at its opening by Chiang Kai-shek, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army; its graduates formed a tight military network, and to be a “Whampoa man” carried the prestige of that origin. Lei Ming and Huang Fen are both of this stamp, which is why each knows the other’s history so well.

Years of the Republic were counted from 1912, so the “sixteenth year” is 1927. Lei is recalling the Northern Expedition’s battles along the Beijing–Hankou (Jinghan) railway that spring, when the Nationalist armies drove north toward Wuhan; the Fourth and Eleventh Armies he names were among its units. The dating quietly measures the present war of 1930 against that earlier, more idealistic campaign, in which Lei fought as a believer.

The war in the background of these chapters is the Central Plains War of 1930, in which Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing government (the “Central Army”) fought the allied forces of Feng Yuxiang’s Northwest Army (西北军) and Yan Xishan of Shanxi, who together had set up a rival “Enlarged Conference” government in the north. The swaying fortunes of that fighting are exactly what drive the government-bond market these men live and die by.

The Dragon-Boat Festival (端阳, the fifth day of the fifth lunar month) was one of the three days of the year on which accounts were traditionally settled and debts called in. Its approach is why Zhu Yinqiu’s bankers are pressing him to clear his loans, and why the speculators reckon the coming squeeze against it.

In 1915–16 Yuan Shikai, the Republic’s first president, proclaimed himself emperor under the reign-title Hongxian (洪宪); the monarchy collapsed within months amid nationwide revolt, and Yuan died soon after. The gibe is that Shang Zhongli is just the sort of court literatus — a “literary attendant” (文学佩从), a scholar kept in waiting on a throne — who would have risen under such a monarchy, and who has since had to make his way “from office into trade.”

ch02.anchor: the golden cicada casting its shell
ch02.note: “The golden cicada casts its shell” (金蝉脱壳) is one of the classic Thirty-Six Stratagems: as the insect leaves an intact empty husk behind, one slips free of danger while leaving a convincing semblance in place. Du Zhuzhai suspects the “bull company” is Zhao Botao’s device for sliding his own exposed long position onto his new partners before the reckoning falls due.

ch03.note: “Dance of death” renders si de tiaowu (死的跳舒), the Chinese for the medieval European danse macabre or Totentanz, the allegory in which Death leads off all ranks of society in a dance. Fan Bowen turns the figure against the revelling rich: their gaiety grows the more frenzied as the countryside collapses around them — a doomed carnival on the very edge of the grave.

“Our Mr. Wang” is Wang Jingwei (汪精卫), leader of the Nationalists’ left-leaning Reorganizationist faction, who in 1930 threw in with the northern coalition against Chiang Kai-shek and its rival ‘Enlarged Conference’ government. Tang Yunshan is his man, and the doctrine preached here — that industrial capital should force politics onto the right track — is the faction’s line. See the note on the Enlarged Conference in Chapter Two.

茨立克, the transliteration of Craven “A”, the cork-tipped Virginia cigarette of Carreras Ltd., a fashionable imported brand in the Shanghai of the day — a small, exact marker of Zhu Yinqiu’s standing even as he pleads poverty.

The slang is hu yu zhuyi (潤浴主义), literally ‘bath-ism,’ from the Wu-dialect hu yu, to take a bath. Zhu Yinqiu, who measures every man by himself, decides that Sun Jiren’s grand talk of running enterprises is really a scheme to slip into the warm water and soak at the shareholders’ expense — to feather his own nest under cover of the bank. The exact force of the phrase is now obscure, and the rendering is provisional.

The May Thirtieth Movement (五半运動) began on 30 May 1925, when British-officered police in the Shanghai International Settlement fired on a Chinese demonstration and killed several; the killings set off nationwide strikes, boycotts and anti-imperialist agitation, a founding moment of the mid-1920s revolution. It was against this ferment that the schoolgirl Lin Peiyao first met the young man now returned as Staff Officer Lei.

Goethe’s Die Leiden des jungen Werthers (1774), the novel of hopeless love and suicide that became a cult across Europe; in Chinese Shaonian Weite zhi fannao (《少年維特之烦恼》), celebrated in Guo Moruo’s 1922 version and a byword among May Fourth youth for romantic feeling. That Staff Officer Lei has carried it, with a pressed white rose, through all his campaigns marks him as a man of that generation’s sentiment.

ch04.note: “Local emperor” renders tu huangdi (土皇帝), the stock name for a rural despot who lorded it over his district as a petty sovereign in his own right — the very class of landlord-gentry the peasant movement of these years set out to break.

ch04.anchor: Down with the local bullies and the evil gentry
ch04.note: “Down with the local bullies and the evil gentry” (dadao tuhao lieshen, 打倒土豪劣绳) was the great rallying-cry of the peasant associations of the late-1920s revolution, aimed at exactly Zeng Canghai’s kind. The flag that goes up with it — “the blue sky, the white sun, and the wholly red earth” (青天白日满地红) — is the national flag of the Republic under the Nationalists, so that the new order’s slogan and its banner reach Shuangqiao together.

An earth-peddler (tu fan, 土販) is a dealer in raw opium, tu (“earth”) being the common slang for the drug. The pun a few lines on — “where there was ‘earth’ there was ‘wealth’” — turns on this: Li Si’s swelling power rests on the opium traffic.

The Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi, 三民主义) — nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood — is the body of doctrine set out by Sun Yat-sen and made the official creed of the Nationalist party and state. The “Premier” to whom Zeng Canghai prays a little later is Sun himself, whom the party revered under that title (zongli). That a rapacious usurer should enshrine the book like a holy relic is the chapter’s sharpest stroke against the new dispensation.

ch04.anchor: Sacred Edict of the old Qing days
ch04.note: The Sacred Edict is the Shengyu Guangxun (圣谋广训, the “Amplified Instructions on the Sacred Edict”), a set of moral maxims issued by the Kangxi and Yongzheng emperors and expounded to the common people at fixed intervals throughout the Qing. Zeng Canghai measures the new party scripture by the old imperial one: to him the Three Principles is simply the Sacred Edict of the present dynasty, an object of compulsory reverence.

Sun Chuanfang (孙传芳, 1885–1935) was the militarist who ruled the five provinces of the lower Yangtze, Shanghai among them, until the Northern Expedition swept him away in 1926–27. To have helped him hunt down and shoot Nationalists is exactly the past that Zeng Canghai, now at the insurgents’ mercy, most needs to disown.

ch05.anchor: better a gap than a makeweight
ch05.note: The maxim is ning que wu lan (宁缺毋滥), “better to leave a place empty than fill it with the unfit.” Wu Sunfu invokes it to justify keeping the weaker capitalists — Zhu Yinqiu, Chen Junyi, Zhou Zhongwei — out of the new combine as partners, even as their factories are marked for “rescue.”

Sun Yat-sen’s Jianguo fanglue (建国方略), a programme for China’s development written 1917–20. Its industrial section proposed a vast “Great Eastern Port” (东方大港) near the mouth of the Yangtze and a national grid of trunk railways; Tang Yunshan, a party man, recites it as scripture. That the plan was still a paper vision in 1930 is the point of Wu Sunfu’s wariness a moment later.

ch05.anchor: Three Fairy Isles upon the sea
ch05.note: The three fabled isles of the immortals — Penglai, Fangzhang and Yingzhou — which old legend set in the eastern sea and which were said to recede as any seeker drew near. The figure casts Sun Yat-sen’s Great Eastern Port and trunk railways as a shimmering mirage, forever promised and never reached.

The quatrain laments the modern spoiling of the West Lake at Hangzhou. The Su Causeway (苏堂) is the willow-planted dyke traditionally credited to the poet Su Shi; the “Lady of the West” renders Xizi (西子), the lake itself, likened ever since Su Shi’s famous couplet to Xi Shi, the great beauty of antiquity. Fan Bowen sets that classical loveliness against the beetle-cars and vulgar villas of the new bourgeoisie.

Fan Bowen’s jibe cuts two ways: in praising the guileless Ah Xuan as more truly “a poet” than a money-god, he means the “Mammon enthroned in his hall of gold” for Wu Sunfu himself, the industrialist in whose house they all sit. Hence the women’s laughter and Wu Sunfu’s scowl — and, a moment later, the barbed question about the silk filature.

Du Xueshi (杜学诗), the sixth of the Du brothers; his given name means literally “study poetry.” Wu Sunfu, who has just sneered at Fan Bowen’s verses, plays on the name — it is Xueshi, “the study of poetry,” who will amount to something — to signal that he would sooner see Peishan matched with the Du brother than with the poet.
